chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from one of our companions, from Ibrahim ibn Khalid, from Abdullah ibn Waddah, from Abu Baseer, who said:

Umm Khalid al-Abdiyyah came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and I was in his presence. So she said, 'May I be sacrificed for you! The growling in my stomach is squeezing me.' She asked him about the ailments of women and said, 'The physicians of Iraq have prescribed Al-Nabeez with Al-Suweq for me, and I paused because I recognized your dislike for it, so I wished to ask you about that.' He said to her, 'And what prevents you from drinking it?' She said, 'I have emulated you in my religion, so when I meet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whenever I meet Him, I can tell Him that Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) ordered me and forbade me.'

He said, 'O Abu Muhammad! Do you listen to this woman and this question? By Allah, I do not grant you permission for one drop of it, and do not taste from it one drop, for you will regret when your soul reaches here.' And he gestured with his hand to his throat, saying it to her three times: 'Did you understand?' She said, 'Yes.'
Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'What wets the needle, dirties a container of water,' saying it to her three times.

key_terms.السَّوِيق: Al-Suweq (a type of flour or grain meal, often used as a base or accompaniment)
key_terms.النَّبِيذ: Al-Nabeez (a specific type of fermented drink, often from dates or grapes)
key_terms.حُبّاً: Hubban (a small amount/container, often referring to a vessel or a handful)
key_terms.قَرَاقِرُ: Qaraqir (growling or gurgling sound in the stomach)
key_terms.قَلَّدْتُكَ دِينِي: Qalladtu ka deeni (I have emulated/followed you in my religion)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on consuming fermented drinks for medical purposes according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Umm Khalid seeks the Imam’s ruling on consuming Al-Nabeez for medicinal purposes, highlighting the Shia principle of *takhassus* (specialization) where the layperson defers to the Imam’s judgment. The Imam’s emphatic prohibition, repeated three times, underscores the severity of wine even when used for cure, while his statement that it 'pollutes water' illustrates the concept of *kathir* (abundant) becoming impure through the addition of a small amount of *qalil* (scant) wine, a key juristic distinction. This narrative reinforces the authority of the Ahl al-Bayt in resolving practical medical and ritual questions, bridging physical health with spiritual purity.
